templates.title: Save rate per pin format and week, each saver of a pin counted once
templates.subtopic: distinct counting at the right grain, first-occurrence attribution, LEFT JOIN of two aggregates

sections.scenario: A product analytics team compares how well each pin format earns saves: standard image pins, video pins, idea pins and product pins. Raw save counts flatter formats whose savers file the same pin onto several boards, so the agreed metric is unique savers per thousand impressions: how many distinct pinners saved each pin, summed over the format's pins, per thousand times those pins were shown. The impression job writes one daily count per pin; the save log has one row per save to a board. You are asked for the weekly table behind a format comparison chart.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns week_start, pin_format, impressions, pin_savers, savers_per_1k, one row per week and format with impressions, ordered by week_start, pin_format. Weeks start on Monday at 00:00 UTC; week_start is that Monday's date. impressions is the sum of the format's daily pin impressions in the week. pin_savers counts distinct (pin, pinner) pairs saved in the week: a pinner who saves one pin to three boards is one saver of that pin, and a pinner who saves two different pins of the format is two. savers_per_1k is 1000 × pin_savers / impressions, rounded to 2 decimal places. A format-week with impressions and no saves is a row with 0 savers. {{week_rule}} {{load_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{pins}} pins and {{saves}} save rows. Every format-week that has a save also has impressions.
sections.assumptions: Formats, counts and the metric are hypothetical and defined for this exercise only; they do not describe any product's reporting. The data holds no information about pinners beyond an opaque id, and the result is aggregated by format.
sections.criteria: Savers counted as distinct (pin, pinner) pairs; impressions and savers aggregated separately and left-joined so zero-saver format-weeks stay; Monday-based UTC weeks; first-save attribution across weeks (Hard+); the latest load per pin-day (Very Hard); correct numeric rounding; deterministic order; can discuss the fairness of a single ratio and incremental first-save state.

clarifications.q: Is a week Monday to Sunday in UTC?
clarifications.a: Yes. A save at Sunday 23:59:59 UTC belongs to the earlier week, one at Monday 00:00:00 to the next.

clarifications.q: One pinner saved the same pin to three boards. How many savers?
clarifications.a: One.

clarifications.q: One pinner saved two different video pins. How many savers?
clarifications.a: Two. The unit is the pair (pin, pinner), not the pinner alone.

clarifications.q: Impressions are per pin and day. Do I count distinct pins?
clarifications.a: No. Sum the daily counts of every pin of the format in the week.

clarifications.q: A format had impressions but nobody saved its pins that week.
clarifications.a: Return it with pin_savers = 0 and savers_per_1k = 0.

clarifications.q: How do I round?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 2) on a numeric, so half away from zero.

hints: Aggregate impressions and savers separately, then join them; joining saves to daily impressions before aggregating multiplies rows.
COUNT(DISTINCT (pin_id, pinner_id)), or reduce saves to one row per pair first, gives savers at the right grain.
Hard: reduce each pair to its first save with MIN(saved_at) before taking the week.
Very Hard: pick each pin-day's latest load with DISTINCT ON (pin_id, impression_date) … ORDER BY …, loaded_at DESC before summing.
followups: The chart should also show the weekly change in savers_per_1k. Add it without a second pass over the data, and say what the first week shows.
Product pins are shown mostly on shopping surfaces. Why can comparing formats by one ratio still mislead, and what would you add to the table to make the comparison fair?
At billions of impressions and saves a week, how would you keep "first save of a pair" correct incrementally, when a pair's first save may have been months ago?
The impression job reloads days when late logs arrive. How would you make the weekly table restate only the weeks that changed, and show readers that a week was restated?

rules.ask: One pinner saves a pin to three boards. What does your count give for that pin, and what does the metric want?
Distinct over pinner alone: one pinner saves two different video pins in a week. How many savers does your query count, and how many should it?
Where does a format with impressions and no saves end up in your result, and in which order are you joining the two aggregates?
Is the format's rate the average of per-pin rates, or total savers over total impressions? What happens to a pin with 20 impressions and 3 savers under each?
Your first save is computed inside the two weeks shown. What happens to a pair whose first save was before the window, and how would you fix that in production?

templates.title: Visual search success per entry point: a save or closeup within 10 minutes
templates.subtopic: time-bounded EXISTS, LEAD to end a window at the next event, counting entities not join rows

sections.scenario: Visual search lets a pinner search with a picture instead of words, and it can be started three ways: the camera, a crop drawn on a pin they are looking at, or an uploaded image. The search team wants to know which entry point leads to searches that help, using a simple proxy agreed for this exercise: a search is successful if the same pinner saves a pin or opens one in closeup within 10 minutes of it. The search log records who searched, how and when, and for a crop the pin it was drawn on. It never stores the image itself, and nothing in this exercise needs it.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns week_start, entry_point, searches, successful_searches, success_rate, one row per week and entry point with at least one search, ordered by week_start, entry_point. Weeks start on Monday at 00:00 UTC; week_start is that Monday's date, taken from searched_at. A search is successful if pin_actions has a save or closeup by the same pinner with action_ts at or after searched_at and at most 10 minutes after it (exactly 10:00 counts). outbound_click never counts. A search counts once however many actions follow it. success_rate is successful_searches / searches rounded to 4 decimal places. {{next_rule}} {{crop_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{searches}} searches and {{actions}} actions. No pinner has two searches at the same instant.
sections.assumptions: Entry points, the 10-minute window and the success proxy are hypothetical and chosen for this exercise; a save or closeup is not proof that a search helped. The tables carry opaque ids only. No image, image feature or inference about the pinner is stored or needed, and results are aggregated by entry point.
sections.criteria: Success decided once per search with EXISTS or an equivalent semi-join; the window inclusive at both ends, same pinner, saves and closeups only; Monday-based UTC weeks from the search time; the window ended at the pinner's next search (Hard+); actions on a crop's source pin excluded (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss the proxy's limits and a streaming version.

clarifications.q: Can an action by a different pinner make a search successful?
clarifications.a: No. Same pinner only.

clarifications.q: An action at exactly 10 minutes after the search?
clarifications.a: It counts. One at 10 minutes and 1 second does not.

clarifications.q: An action a minute before the search?
clarifications.a: It does not follow the search, so it does not count.

clarifications.q: Does an outbound click count?
clarifications.a: No. Only save and closeup.

clarifications.q: A search followed by a closeup and then a save?
clarifications.a: One successful search.

clarifications.q: How is the rate rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) on a numeric.

hints: Decide success per search first (one row per search with a boolean), then aggregate; a plain join to actions multiplies searches.
EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pin_actions a WHERE a.pinner_id = s.pinner_id AND … ) with both window bounds is the simplest correct shape.
Hard: LEAD(searched_at) OVER (PARTITION BY pinner_id ORDER BY searched_at) gives each search's next search; the action must come strictly before it.
followups: Product asks for the median time from search to first save per entry point. Change your query, and say what happens to searches with no save.
The 10-minute proxy is arbitrary. How would you choose the window from data, and how would you check that the comparison between entry points does not flip with it?
Camera searches are mostly on phones and uploads mostly on the web. How would you separate the effect of the entry point from the effect of the device?
At hundreds of millions of searches a week, the EXISTS becomes a large range join. How would you compute success in a stream, and what state does each pinner need?

rules.ask: A search has a closeup and a save inside the window. How many rows does your join produce for it, and how do you count it once?
BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends. Which of your two bounds should be inclusive here, and does the next-search bound need to be exclusive?
An action happens at exactly the same second as the pinner's next search. Which search does your query give it to?
You add an interval to a timestamptz. Would anything change if the session time zone were not UTC, for the window or for the week?
The success metric needs none of that. What would storing the pinner's image add to the risk, and what would you keep instead?

templates.title: Fresh-pin share of home feed impressions, a repin as old as its original
templates.subtopic: self-join to the original row, strict interval boundaries, deduplicating retried logs

sections.scenario: A home feed team wants to know how much of what pinners see is fresh: recently created ideas rather than pins that have circulated for years. Which pins the feed shows is decided by a scoring function you are given and is out of scope here; this question only measures what was shown. The catch is repins: when a pinner saves an existing pin, a new pin row is created that points to the original, so a repin made an hour ago can carry an idea that is two years old. For this exercise's rule (hypothetical, agreed with the team), a repin is as old as its original.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns impression_date, country, impressions, fresh_impressions, fresh_share, one row per UTC date of impression_ts and country, ordered by impression_date, country. An impression is fresh if it happened less than {{fresh_days}} days (exactly {{fresh_days}} × 24 hours) after the start of its pin's original: for an original pin (original_pin_id is NULL) that is the pin itself; for a repin it is the pin original_pin_id points to, which is always an original. An impression exactly {{fresh_days}} days after the start is not fresh. fresh_share is fresh_impressions / impressions, rounded to 4 decimal places. {{sched_rule}} {{dup_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{pins}} pins and {{logs}} impression log rows. original_pin_id never points to another repin.
sections.assumptions: Pins, countries, counts and the freshness rule are hypothetical; they do not describe how any feed ranks or reports. Country is the viewer's country as logged with the impression, used only for this aggregate; the data holds no information about who saw the pin.
sections.criteria: Every impression dated by its original's start through COALESCE(original_pin_id, pin_id); a strict upper bound at exactly {{fresh_days}} days; UTC dates from the impression; duplicates counted once by impression_id (Hard+); the scheduled publish time as the start (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss repin chains, seasonal relevance without profiling, and the join at scale.

clarifications.q: A repin created yesterday of a pin created last year: fresh?
clarifications.a: No. It is as old as its original.

clarifications.q: What exactly is the window?
clarifications.a: Strictly less than {{fresh_days}} × 24 hours between the original's start and the impression. At exactly that difference it is no longer fresh.

clarifications.q: Which day does an impression belong to?
clarifications.a: The UTC date of impression_ts.

clarifications.q: Can a repin point to another repin?
clarifications.a: Not in this data: original_pin_id always names an original.

clarifications.q: How is the share rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) on a numeric.

hints: Join each impression's pin to its original with COALESCE(original_pin_id, pin_id), then compare times on the original.
Write the window as impression_ts < start + INTERVAL '… days', so the boundary is exclusive by construction.
Hard: reduce the log to one row per impression_id before counting.
Very Hard: the original's start is COALESCE(published_at, created_at).
followups: The team also wants the share of impressions that showed a repin rather than an original, per country and day. Add it, and say why it is a different question from freshness.
Suppose original_pin_id could point to another repin (a chain of saves). What changes in your query, and how deep can chains get before it matters?
Freshness by creation time penalises an old idea that becomes relevant again each season. How would you define and measure "fresh to this pinner" without profiling anyone, using only aggregates?
The impression log is billions of rows a day and the pins table is billions of rows. How would you avoid joining the whole pins table every day?

rules.ask: A repin made an hour ago of a pin from last year: which creation time does your query compare against, and what does the rule say?
An impression lands exactly {{fresh_days}} days after the original's start. Does your query call it fresh, and should it?
That fixes the total. Does your fresh count also dedupe, or can a retried fresh impression still be counted twice?
Is adding a day-based interval to a timestamptz always 24 hours? When would it not be, and why is it safe here?
The data guarantees one hop. What would a recursive CTE cost on a billion-row pins table, and how would you store the root instead?

templates.title: Distinct savers of a pin over many date ranges
templates.subtopic: sorting queries by right end, last occurrence per key, Fenwick tree

sections.scenario: A creator looking at their own pin's analytics can pick any date range and see how many different pinners saved it in that range: a launch week, a holiday season, the months since a redesign. Saves are not unique per pinner (people save the same pin to several boards, or again a year later), so the number is a distinct count, and distinct counts do not add up across days. A nightly job precomputes the answers for the ranges creators look at most, tens of thousands of ranges over years of saves, and it has to finish in seconds.
sections.problem: Implement distinct_savers(saves, queries). Each save is (pin_id, day, pinner_id); day is a whole day number. Each query is (pin_id, first_day, last_day). Return a list with one integer per query, in query order: the number of distinct pinners who saved that pin on at least one day from first_day to last_day, both inclusive. {{order_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 saves, 50 000 queries and 3 000 distinct days; ranges are long (a third of the data on average). Building a set of pinners for each range is far too slow; aim for O((n + q) log n).
sections.assumptions: Pins, pinners, days and volumes are hypothetical. Pinner ids are opaque; the result is a count, shown only to the pin's own creator, and never says who saved.
sections.criteria: Recognises that distinct counts are not prefix-subtractable; offline sweep by right end with each pinner's latest save marked; a Fenwick tree (or segment tree) for the count; O((n + q) log n); inclusive bounds; answers returned in input order; repeated saves, empty ranges and unordered input handled (Hard); per-pin separation and unknown pins (Very Hard); can discuss online queries and approximate sketches.

clarifications.q: A pinner saved the pin three times in the range.
clarifications.a: One pinner.

clarifications.q: A pinner saved inside the range and again after it. Do they count?
clarifications.a: Yes. One save inside the range is enough.

clarifications.q: Are both ends inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. (pin, 5, 5) asks about day 5 only.

clarifications.q: Can I answer the queries in a different order than given?
clarifications.a: Yes, as long as the returned list follows the input order.

clarifications.q: Do I need to support new saves arriving between queries?
clarifications.a: No. Everything is known up front; the job is offline.

hints: Distinct counts do not subtract: count(1..b) − count(1..a−1) is wrong, because a pinner can appear on both sides.
Sort the queries by last_day and sweep the saves in day order. For each pinner, only their latest save so far matters.
Mark each pinner's latest save day with a 1 (and remove the mark from their previous latest day). For a query ending at the current day, the answer is the number of marks on days ≥ first_day.
A Fenwick (binary indexed) tree over the distinct days gives both the update and the "marks before first_day" count in O(log D).
followups: Prove that counting latest saves on days ≥ first_day gives exactly the distinct pinners in the range, once all saves up to last_day have been swept.
The dashboard is interactive: ranges arrive one at a time and must be answered immediately. What changes, and what does a persistent segment tree buy you?
Creators accept "about 12 400" for very large pins. How would an approximate distinct count (for example HyperLogLog sketches per day) answer arbitrary ranges, and how large is the error?
Saves can be deleted when a pinner removes a pin from a board. Should the count change, and how would your structure handle deletions?

rules.ask: How many pinners does your set hold for an average range, and how many ranges are there? What is the total work?
A pinner saved on day 3 and day 9. Your prefix counts for 1..9 and 1..4 both include them. What does subtracting give for the range 5..9?
What is the cost of moving the window in your order, and how does it compare with a single sweep by right end?
Your tree is indexed by what: save rows, day numbers or distinct days? What does that choice cost in memory over three years of saves?
Can you merge sketches for an arbitrary range quickly, and what is the error for a range with 50 savers?

templates.title: Busier-day lookback: days back to the last day with more saves
templates.subtopic: previous strictly greater element with a monotonic stack, grouping and summing rows per key

sections.scenario: A creator's analytics page annotates each day of a pin's history with a short note: "best day in 41 days", or "best day ever" when no earlier day beat it. Evergreen pins collect saves for years (recipes, home projects, seasonal ideas), so a pin's history can run to thousands of days, and the nightly job annotates every pin a creator owns. The annotation is the distance back to the most recent earlier day that had more saves.
sections.problem: Implement busier_lookback(rows). Each row is (pin_id, day, saves): day is a whole day number and saves the number of saves that day. Return a dict mapping every pin to a list with one integer per listed day of that pin, in increasing day order: day − d, where d is the latest earlier listed day of the same pin with strictly more saves, or 0 if no earlier day had more. A day with the same number of saves is not busier. {{day_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 100 pins of 3 000 days each in one call. Many pins open with a busy launch day and then climb slowly, with long stretches of equal days, so scanning back from each day is quadratic; aim for O(n) after grouping (O(n log n) if you sort).
sections.assumptions: Pins and save counts are hypothetical. The result describes a pin, is shown only to that pin's own creator, and uses daily totals, never who saved.
sections.criteria: A monotonic stack per pin (or an equivalent amortised linear method) for the previous strictly greater day; <= when popping so equal days are skipped; 0 when the stack is empty; O(n) per pin after grouping; calendar-day differences with gaps (Hard+); summed duplicate days and unordered rows (Very Hard); pins kept separate; can prove the stack invariant and extend it forward and incrementally.

clarifications.q: Two days with the same saves: is the earlier one busier?
clarifications.a: No. Strictly more saves only.

clarifications.q: What do I return for the first day of a pin?
clarifications.a: 0: no earlier day exists.

clarifications.q: Could the answer be 0 for a reason other than "no busier day"?
clarifications.a: No. A busier day is always at least one day earlier, so 0 only ever means none.

clarifications.q: Do pins affect each other?
clarifications.a: No. Each pin's history is separate.

clarifications.q: Is the output in day order?
clarifications.a: Yes, one value per listed day of the pin, from its first day to its last.

hints: For each day, which earlier days can ever be the answer for a later day? A day followed by a day with at least as many saves can never be the answer again.
Keep a stack of (day, saves) whose saves strictly decrease from bottom to top. Pop while the top has saves ≤ today's; whatever is left on top is the busier day.
Each day is pushed and popped at most once, so the pass is linear per pin.
Hard and Very Hard: group rows per pin into a dict of day → summed saves first, then sort the days.
followups: Prove the stack never discards a day that some later day needs.
Creators also want "best day in N days" for the next busier day forward ("held the record for 12 days"). How do you compute both in one or two passes?
Annotations are recomputed nightly for every pin. Most pins gain one new day. How would you update the stored stack incrementally instead of recomputing years of history?
The same lookback across all pins of a board (summing pins per day) is requested. What changes, and what breaks if pins are added to the board later?

rules.ask: A pin has a launch spike on day 1 and then climbs slowly for six years. How many comparisons does your scan do for the last day, and in total?
A running maximum answers "best day ever". What does it tell you for a day that is not a record, and what do you still have to find?
When you pop, is the condition < or <=? What goes wrong for equal days with the other one?
Is the lookback the difference in list positions or in day numbers? When are they different?
That works in O(n log n). What does the stack give you that it does not, and is it worth the memory?

templates.title: Price-drop alerts on saved product pins
templates.subtopic: event sweep with a max-heap of pending thresholds per product

sections.scenario: Product pins show an item from a merchant's catalogue with its current price. When a pinner saves a product pin, they may want to hear when it gets cheaper. A daily job reads the catalogue's price history and every save of a product pin, and for each save it finds the day the product first became cheap enough to send one alert. Popular products are saved by many pinners on many different days, and catalogue prices move a little almost every day, so most saves wait a long time before anything happens.
sections.problem: Implement price_drop_alerts(saves, prices, pct=90). saves is a list of (product, day), one per save, where day is an integer day number. prices is a list of (product, day, price) rows in any order, with price in integer cents. A row's price holds from its day until that product's next row, and a product has at most one row per day. The price on a save is the price in force on the save day, including a row dated that same day. A save alerts on the first day after the save day whose price is at most pct per cent of the price on the save. The comparison is exact: 100 × price ≤ pct × saved price. Return one integer per save, in the order of saves: the alert day, or -1 if the price never gets that low, or if the product had no price yet on the save day. {{pct_rule}} {{stock_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 150 000 saves and up to 80 000 price rows in the timing check, over 20 products with 4 000 days of history. Prices wobble by a few per cent, so most saves stay pending for thousands of days. A scan forward from each save through its product's later rows is O(s·d) and too slow. Something close to O((s + d) log s) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Products, prices, days and the alert percentage are hypothetical; the 90% default is this exercise's rule, so check current docs for how any real alert works. One save gets at most one alert. Days are whole days in one time zone, and price rows are already validated. Nothing about the pinner is needed beyond the save itself.
sections.criteria: Saved price taken from the row in force on the save day, including a same-day row; alerts only on later days; the first qualifying day, not the cheapest; the exact integer comparison at the boundary; -1 for saves before the first price; independent products; at Very Hard, out-of-stock days never alert and saves while out of stock return -1; an event sweep with a per-product max-heap (or another O(log) structure) rather than a scan per save; a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on deduplication, incremental runs and bad feed data.

clarifications.q: Does a cheaper price on the save day itself trigger an alert?
clarifications.a: No. A row dated the save day sets the saved price. Only later days can alert.

clarifications.q: Is exactly pct per cent enough?
clarifications.a: Yes. The rule is 100 × price ≤ pct × saved price, in integers, so there is no rounding question.

clarifications.q: Do I report the cheapest day or the first qualifying day?
clarifications.a: The first qualifying day. The alert goes out as soon as the price is low enough.

clarifications.q: What if the product has no price row on or before the save day?
clarifications.a: There is no saved price, so that save never alerts: -1.

clarifications.q: Are the rows sorted?
clarifications.a: No. Rows for different products are interleaved and out of order.

hints: Process days in order. Within a day, apply that day's price rows before that day's saves, so a save never alerts on its own day.
For one product, which pending save alerts first when the price falls? The one with the highest threshold. Keep pending saves in a max-heap by pct × saved price.
When a price arrives, pop from that product's heap while the top threshold is at least 100 × price. Every pop is an alert on that day, and each save is popped at most once.
followups: Pinners save the same product more than once, on different boards. How would you send at most one alert per pinner and product, and which save's price would you use?
The job runs every day on the newest prices only. What state do you keep between runs, and how big does it get for a product saved by millions of pinners?
A merchant's feed sends a wrong price of one cent for an hour, then corrects it. How do you avoid a wave of false alerts, and what would you check before sending?
The catalogue changes currency for a region, so prices in one product's history are in two currencies. What breaks in your comparison, and how would you fix the data model?

rules.ask: A popular product has 10 000 pending saves and a price row every day for ten years. How many comparisons does your loop make?
Why is the top of the heap the right save to test first? What would you have to change if the threshold depended on the pinner, not only on the saved price?
Your threshold is computed with a float. Give a price where price <= 0.9 * saved and the integer rule disagree, or explain why they cannot.
After sorting, what do you do with a save whose product drops on the same day it was saved?
That finds the first cheap enough day for one save in log time. How does it compare with a sweep for memory and for a daily incremental run?

templates.title: Order agreement between shown pins and a given scoring function
templates.subtopic: counting discordant pairs (inversions) with ties and duplicates

sections.scenario: An offline evaluation compares two orderings of the same pins. One is the order in which a long list of pins was actually shown, taken from impression logs. The other is the order that a scoring function you are given would produce, where a higher score means the pin would be placed higher. The team wants one number that says how much the two disagree: the number of pairs of pins that were shown in the opposite order from the one the scoring function prefers. Lists for broad interests run to hundreds of thousands of pins, and the job runs for many of them.
sections.problem: Implement discordant_pairs(shown, scores, report_comparable=False). shown is a list of pin ids in the order they were shown, first position first. scores maps a pin id to its integer score. A pair of two different counted pins a and b is discordant when a was shown before b but scores[a] < scores[b]. Return the number of discordant pairs. {{data_rule}} {{return_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 380 000 shown pins in the timing check. Scores are integers and may be negative. Comparing every pair is about 10¹¹ comparisons. Something close to O(n log n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Pin ids, scores and lists are hypothetical. The scoring function is given and treated as a black box: this exercise does not say how any real ranking is built, and it does not look at who saw the pins. The count can exceed 32 bits.
sections.criteria: Correct direction of disagreement; repeated pins counted once at their first position; unscored pins skipped; equal scores never counted as discordant; at Very Hard, comparable pairs counted as all pairs minus pairs within equal-score groups; an O(n log n) count by merge sort or a Fenwick tree over score ranks; a clear explanation of tie handling; awareness that the count can exceed 32 bits; sensible answers on normalisation, position weighting and incremental counting.

clarifications.q: Which direction is discordant?
clarifications.a: The pin shown earlier has the lower score. If the earlier pin has the higher score, the pair agrees.

clarifications.q: Do I need to produce the scoring function's order?
clarifications.a: No. You need only the count of pairs where the two orders disagree.

clarifications.q: What do I return when nothing is shown?
clarifications.a: Zero, because there are no pairs (or (0, 0) when comparable pairs are reported too).

clarifications.q: Are scores unique?
clarifications.a: Only where the statement says so. Otherwise equal scores happen, and a pair with equal scores is not discordant.

clarifications.q: Can the answer be large?
clarifications.a: Yes, close to n²/2 for a reversed list. Python integers handle it. Say what you would use in a language with fixed-width integers.

hints: List the counted scores in shown order. A discordant pair is a pair of positions i < j with v[i] < v[j]. That is an inversion count with the comparison reversed.
Merge sort the list into descending order. When an element from the right half is placed before the remaining elements of the left half, each of those left elements was earlier and smaller.
With equal scores, take the left element first on a tie, so equal pairs are never counted. For comparable pairs, count all pairs and subtract the pairs inside each group of equal scores.
followups: The team wants a normalised number between −1 and 1 that is comparable across lists of different lengths. Which statistic would you report, and how do ties change its denominator?
Disagreements near the top of the list matter more than disagreements at position 40 000. How would you weight pairs by position, and does your algorithm still work?
Lists are now produced continuously, and the team wants the count for the last hour's impressions only. What would you keep incrementally?
The scoring function is run on a sample of pins only, and the rest have no score. How do the skipped pins bias the agreement number, and how would you report that?

rules.ask: Each insort shifts the elements after the insertion point. How many element moves does that make for 380 000 pins in random order?
Your tree is indexed by score. Scores are large and may be negative. How do you map them to indexes, and what happens with equal scores?
On a tie between a left and a right element, which do you take first, and what count goes wrong if you take the other one?
How long do 10¹¹ comparisons take in CPython? What is the largest list you could handle in the time limit?
A pin appears at positions 3 and 900. Which position does your code keep, and why does that matter for the count?

templates.title: Debug the pin engagement rollup
templates.subtopic: repin credit, visibility rules, deletions, units and week boundaries

sections.scenario: Creators see weekly impressions, saves and views for each pin they published. A save creates a repin on the saver's board, and the engagement a repin gets is credited to the original pin. Creators and analysts have raised several complaints about one weekly rollup. Pins saved through a chain of repins show engagement on someone else's repin instead of on the original. Pins that are popular with group boards look less saved than they should. A deleted pin still shows up in reports, while a pin whose repin was deleted loses engagement it really had. Video views look far too high next to the player's own numbers. Weekly totals do not match the UTC dashboards in the first hours of every Monday. The rollup below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix weekly_engagement(events, pins) so that it meets this specification. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Pins. pins maps a pin id to {"origin", "format", "deleted"}. origin is the pin it was saved from, or None for an original pin. A repin's origin may itself be a repin, and its format ("static" or "video") is the same as its original's. An event for a pin that is not in pins is ignored.
  2. Credit. Every event is credited to its pin's original: follow origin until it is None. A deleted repin's events still count for the original. If the original is deleted, none of its events are reported.
  3. Metrics. An impression adds 1 to impressions. A save adds 1 to saves unless board is "secret": saves to public and group boards count. A closeup adds 1 to views when the original is static. A video_view adds 1 to views when the original is a video and watched_ms is at least 2 000 (2 seconds, this exercise's rule). A closeup on a video pin is not a view.
  4. Weeks. ts is Unix seconds. A week starts on Monday at 00:00 UTC and is labelled by that Monday's date, YYYY-MM-DD.
  5. Output. A dict keyed "<original>|<week>", each value {"impressions", "saves", "views"}. A key appears only if at least one event counted for it.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 events and 20 000 pins, processed in close to linear time.
sections.assumptions: Event types, fields and the 2-second rule are hypothetical and simplified; check current docs for how any real metric is defined. Events are already deduplicated. Secret-board saves are private to the pinner and never appear in creator metrics.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its creator-facing symptom; credit follows the whole repin chain; secret saves excluded and group saves kept; deletion checked on the original, not on the event's pin; the view threshold compared in matching units; Monday weeks in UTC; minimal fixes that keep the output format; a regression test per bug.

clarifications.q: Does a repin of a repin go to the middle pin or to the first one?
clarifications.a: To the original, the first pin in the chain.

clarifications.q: What about group boards?
clarifications.a: They are not secret. Saves to group boards count like saves to public boards.

clarifications.q: A repin was deleted. Do its earlier saves disappear from the original's numbers?
clarifications.a: No. They happened, and they are credited to the original. Only a deleted original removes its rows.

clarifications.q: Which time zone defines a week?
clarifications.a: UTC. A week runs from Monday 00:00:00 to Sunday 23:59:59 UTC.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Draw a chain of three pins, original → repin → repin of repin, and put an event on the last one. Where does the code credit it?
List the board values a save can have, and the ones the code counts.
Read every unit and constant next to the comparison that uses it.
Take an impression at Monday 03:00 UTC and work out by hand which week the code gives it.
followups: Creators can see their own pins' weekly numbers, but the same table feeds a public trends page. Which rows or counts must never reach the public page, and where would you enforce that?
A pin's original is deleted, and the creator asks for last month's report again. Should the old numbers change? What would you store to answer both ways?
Events arrive up to three days late. How would you rerun a week without double counting, and when would you call a week final?
Repin chains are long and the rollup follows them for every event. How would you precompute the original for every pin, and keep it current as pins are created and deleted?

rules.ask: A chain is 10 000 repins long. What does your code do, and how would you avoid walking it for every event?
Your cache maps a pin to its original. What must happen to it when an original pin is deleted, or when a new repin is created?
Creators in different countries want weeks in their own time zone. What do you store so that both UTC and local weeks can be produced?
A new board type is added next quarter. Does your check count it or drop it by default, and which default is safer for creator metrics?
Where else in a pipeline like this do seconds and milliseconds meet, and how would a test catch the next one?

templates.title: Visual search request logging that never stores the pinner's photo
templates.subtopic: privacy by design, derived features only, joins to later actions

entry_points: camera, crop on a pin and uploaded image
crop on a pin and camera

sections.scenario: Visual search lets a pinner search with an image instead of words. The entry points are {{entry_points}}. The service detects objects in the image, the pinner can adjust a crop, and results are served as a grid of pins. There are about {{daily_searches}} visual searches a day. The product team wants to know which entry points and detected object kinds lead to useful results, measured by what the pinner did within {{followup_window}}: a closeup, a save or an outbound click. The rule for this log is strict: the pinner's photo, from the camera or uploaded, is never stored, not even briefly in a debug table.
sections.problem: Design the logging and analytics pipeline for visual search. Cover the request event and what it may and may not contain, the crops and detected objects, the results served with their positions, the later actions and how they are joined to the request, how crops on public pins differ from the pinner's own photo, retention for {{retention}}, the aggregates the product team uses, and how you prove that no photo or photo-derived identifier is kept.
sections.constraints: No pixels, thumbnails or reversible image embeddings of the pinner's own photo may be logged or kept. Joins to later actions must not depend on a long-lived identifier of the pinner. Reports are aggregates by entry point, object kind, country and week, with small cells suppressed. Late and duplicate client events are normal. Logs older than {{retention}} are deleted.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, windows, retention and the list of entry points are hypothetical. Object detection returns a label from a fixed list (for example "chair", "lamp", "dress") with a bounding box and a confidence. Results are pins and product pins identified by public pin ids. Any real product's logging rules may differ; check current docs.
sections.criteria: A schema that excludes the pinner's photo and anything reversible derived from it; crops on public pins logged by pin id and box; a short-lived request id rather than a pinner id for joins; a clear definition of useful with the {{followup_window}} window and late events; deduplication of client retries; aggregate reports with small-cell suppression; retention enforced and verified; automated checks on schema and samples that would catch a leak; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: May we keep an embedding of the photo to debug bad results?
clarifications.a: Not of the pinner's own photo. An embedding can often be inverted or matched back to the image, so it counts as the photo. A crop on a public pin can be logged by pin id and box.

clarifications.q: How do later actions find their search?
clarifications.a: That is part of your design. A short-lived request id issued by the server and echoed by the client is one option.

clarifications.q: Do we need per-pinner history?
clarifications.a: No. The questions are about entry points and object kinds in aggregate, and nothing is inferred about the pinner.

clarifications.q: What does "useful" mean?
clarifications.a: A closeup, save or outbound click on a served result within {{followup_window}} of the results being shown.

clarifications.q: Can the detected labels be sensitive?
clarifications.a: The label list is fixed to objects and products. If a label could describe a person, it is not on the list and is never logged.

hints: Split the request into what came from the pinner (an image you must not keep) and what the service produced (labels, boxes, result ids). Log only the second kind.
Use a request id that is generated per search and expires with the {{followup_window}} join, rather than a pinner id.
Decide where the photo exists at all (memory on the serving path only) and write the rule as a test that scans the logged schema and samples.
followups: A bug report says results are bad for chairs photographed in dim light. How do engineers investigate without the photos?
A client release starts sending the image hash with every search event. How do you detect it, stop it and delete what was written?
The team wants to know whether repeat users of visual search save more over a month. What would you need, and is it compatible with this log's rules?
Volume grows tenfold from {{daily_searches}} a day, and a new video-frame entry point is added. What changes in the pipeline and in the privacy checks?

rules.ask: You log a vector computed from the pinner's photo. How would someone match it back to the image, and what would you log instead?
Which question needs that identifier? Could a per-search request id that expires answer it instead?
What exactly is written to that bucket, who can read it, and how long does it live?
The save event arrives 40 minutes later because the phone was offline. Does it still join, and should it count?
Which cells fall below your threshold most often, and how do you avoid revealing them by subtraction from totals?

incidents: A client release adds a base64 thumbnail to the error event of failed visual searches; it reaches the raw log for six hours before anyone notices.
A client retry bug sends every results-served event twice for one day, so served results double for every entry point while actions do not.
Deletion of logs older than {{retention}} fails silently for a week because a partition was renamed.

templates.title: Saves from the browser extension and the mobile share sheet
templates.subtopic: client-generated ids, out-of-order and duplicate events, source attribution

clients: browser extension and mobile share sheet
browser extension, mobile share sheet and website save button

sections.scenario: Pinners save images from other websites through the {{clients}}. Each save creates a new pin that records the page it came from, and creators who claimed that website can later see saves from their pages. There are about {{daily_saves}} such saves a day. Mobile clients queue saves while offline for up to {{offline_hours}} hours and send them later, sometimes twice. Edits and deletes of a just-created pin can arrive before the save itself. Analysts want a clean table of saves from external pages, with the source page, the client and the time the pinner actually saved.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from the client's save request to the analytics table. Cover the identity of a save across retries, how out-of-order create, edit and delete events are applied, how the source page URL is normalised and recorded, which time is the save time, how late events from offline clients reach past days, what the analytics table looks like and how it is kept correct when a pin is deleted.
sections.constraints: A retried save must never create two pins or two analytics rows. A pin deleted by its pinner must disappear from the analytics table within a day. Source URLs can carry tracking parameters and session tokens that must not be stored. Client clocks can be wrong by hours. Daily reports must be re-runnable for any past day.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, offline periods and client list are hypothetical. Each client can generate a random id when the pinner taps save. The service records its own receive time. Any real product's behaviour may differ; check current docs.
sections.criteria: A client-minted save id used for idempotent creation; versioned records with tombstones so out-of-order deletes win; a defensible save-time rule with client and server times kept; URL normalisation that removes tracking and session parameters, versioned and re-runnable; late events written to their day with reruns that overwrite partitions; deletion propagated to analytics within a day; creator views in aggregate only; a bounded deduplication window; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Which time is the save time, the phone's or the server's?
clarifications.a: Analysts want when the pinner saved, but phone clocks can be wrong. You decide, and you must say how you handle a phone that is hours off.

clarifications.q: Can a delete arrive before its create?
clarifications.a: Yes, when the pinner deletes a pin created offline and the events are sent in a different order.

clarifications.q: Which part of the URL is the source page?
clarifications.a: The page without fragments, tracking parameters or session tokens. Decide how you normalise it, and keep the rule versioned.

clarifications.q: Do creators see who saved?
clarifications.a: No. Creators see counts of saves from their claimed pages, never the pinners.

clarifications.q: What if the same image is saved from two different pages?
clarifications.a: Those are two saves with two source pages.

hints: Let the client mint a save id when the pinner taps save, and make it the key for creating the pin, so a retry finds the existing pin.
Treat create, edit and delete as versions of one record keyed by save id, and keep a tombstone so that a create arriving after a delete stays deleted.
Record both the client time and the server receive time, and derive a save time with a rule you can explain.
followups: A client bug reuses the same save id for every save made in one offline session. What do you see in the data, and how do you repair it?
A website changes its URL structure, and creators see their saves split across two pages. How does your normalisation handle it, and can you re-normalise history?
The daily report for a day 3 days ago changes because offline saves arrived late. How do you rerun it, and what do analysts see?
At {{daily_saves}} a day, the deduplication store becomes the bottleneck. How do you bound it, and what happens to a retry that arrives after the window?

rules.ask: The client generates the id. What happens if two phones generate the same one, and how would you detect it?
A save made on Saturday offline arrives on Monday. Which day's report does it belong to, and how do you justify that to analysts?
A delete with an older client timestamp arrives after an edit with a newer one. What does your merge decide, and is that right?
Which parts of the URL do you keep? Show one parameter that must be removed for privacy and one that may change the page.
Where exactly is the duplicate dropped: at the API, in the stream or in the table? What does each choice cost?

incidents: After a mobile release, offline queues of up to {{offline_hours}} hours flush at once and every save is sent twice.
A browser extension version sends the full page URL with a session token in the query string for two days.
Deletes for pins created offline arrive before their creates for one client version, and those pins reappear in the analytics table.

templates.title: Pins, saves and boards as data — original pins, saves to boards and sections, and credit to the original creator
templates.subtopic: save lineage, root-pin credit, board visibility history, deletions

sections.scenario: A creator publishes an original pin: an image or video with a title, a description and usually a link to a web page. Pinners save pins to their own boards, optionally into a section of a board, and the saved copy can itself be saved by someone else from that board, so a popular pin spreads through long chains of saves. A saver can edit the description on their copy, move it to another board or section, or delete it. Boards are public or secret (about {{secret_share}} of saves land on secret boards here), and about {{group_share}} of saves go to group boards that several collaborators save to. In this exercise's rule, every save of a copy anywhere in a chain counts as a save of the original pin and is credited to its creator, saves to secret boards are left out of public counts and of creator analytics, and a deleted pin or board must disappear from analytics within {{deletion_days}} days. About {{daily_saves}} saves happen a day.
sections.problem: Design the data model, from the transactional entities to the analytical facts. Cover: pins (original versus saved copy) and how each copy points back to the original it descends from; boards, sections, collaborators and board visibility with its history; saves as events versus the current contents of a board; moves between boards and sections; edits to a copy's description; deletions of a copy, a board, or the original itself. Then define the facts and their grains that answer "saves of a creator's original pins per day", "where saves came from (which surface or board the pinner saved from)", and "the public save count shown on a pin", and write one definition of a "save" that the creator dashboard and the public count can share, with the secret-board rule applied.
sections.constraints: Credit always reaches the original pin and its creator in one step, however long the chain. A save on a secret board never appears in a public count, a public board listing or a creator's analytics, including after the board's visibility changes. Re-saving a copy you already saved to the same board is not a new save. History is kept: a creator's daily saves for a past day change only through deletion (documented) or a stated restatement. Deletions reach analytics within {{deletion_days}} days.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares and the deletion window are hypothetical. Every pin has exactly one original, which may be itself. A copy's link and image are those of its original; only the title and description can be edited. Collaborators of a group board can save to it and remove what they saved; the owner can remove anything.
sections.criteria: Root and parent kept on every copy, with credit by root; saves as append-only events and board contents as derived state; board visibility with history and a stated rule for which visibility judges a save; moves and description edits that are not new saves; idempotent saves per pinner, board and original; deletion of a copy, board or original propagated within the window with a documented effect on past totals; facts at stated grains (save events, creator × original × day, public count) built from one save definition; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does saving a copy credit the pinner whose board it came from?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. The creator of the original is credited; the intermediate saver can see, in aggregate, that pins were saved from their board.

clarifications.q: Does a move between boards count as a new save?
clarifications.a: No. A move changes where a saved copy lives; the save happened once.

clarifications.q: A board changes from secret to public. Do its earlier saves start counting?
clarifications.a: That is your decision; state it. The constraint is that a save made while the board was secret never appears anywhere public.

clarifications.q: What happens to copies when the original pin is deleted?
clarifications.a: In this exercise the copies stay on pinners' boards, but the original's creator analytics stop including them once the deletion has been applied.

clarifications.q: Can one pinner save the same original to several boards?
clarifications.a: Yes. Each is a save; say whether a "unique savers" measure also exists and how it is computed.

hints: Store the original on every copy (a root pin id) as well as the copy it was saved from (a parent). Credit reads the root; provenance reads the parent.
Keep saves as append-only events and board contents as current state derived from them; visibility belongs to the board and needs its own history.
Decide which board visibility a save is judged by: the board's visibility at the moment of the save, or now. Write it down before designing the fact.
followups: Draw the rows for: a creator's original A; pinner P saves A to board B1; pinner Q saves P's copy to B2 (secret); Q later moves it to B3 (public). What does each fact show?
A chain is a million copies deep for a viral pin. How does your model avoid walking the chain to find the creator, and what guards against a copy whose root is wrong?
The original pin is deleted. Which rows change, within {{deletion_days}} days, and how do the creator's past daily totals change?
A group board's owner removes a collaborator and everything they saved. What happens to save counts and to the collaborator's own history?

Define the public save count precisely (which events add, which subtract, what secret boards do) and show that the creator dashboard can be derived from the same events at about {{daily_saves}} saves a day.

rules.ask: To credit the creator you need the original. Do you walk parent links at query time, and what does that cost on a chain of thousands of saves?
A save is made on a secret board, then the board turns public. Does your counter change, and how do you rebuild it if it drifts?
Which visibility decides whether a save counts: the board's visibility when the save happened, or today's? Show what happens to a save made while the board was secret.
The original is deleted. Which tables keep rows, which facts drop them within {{deletion_days}} days, and what can still be seen by whom?
Unique savers across days do not add up. Which grain stores them, and what does the creator see for a week?

incidents: A board with thousands of pins switched from secret to public, and the next morning its owner's earlier secret saves showed up in several creators' weekly save totals: the job joined saves to the board's current visibility.

A group board's owner removed a collaborator and everything they had saved (group boards take about {{group_share}} of saves here). A backfill that found the original by walking parent links stopped at the deleted copies, and for a day the saves made from them were credited to the removed collaborator instead of the original creators.
A bulk import re-saved the same pins to the same boards after a client retry, and save counts for affected pins doubled within a day at {{daily_saves}} saves a day.

templates.title: Idea pins as data — pages, media, tags, edits after publishing and engagement per page
templates.subtopic: versioned multi-part content, stable page identity, per-page engagement

sections.scenario: Creators publish idea pins: a pin made of up to {{max_pages}} pages, each page an image or a short video (about {{video_share}} of pages are video here) with optional text overlays. A creator adds topic tags, can tag other creators and products on a page, and can list ingredients or materials on the pin. After publishing, a creator can edit: change text, replace a page's media, add, remove or reorder pages, or change the tags; about {{edited_share}} of idea pins are edited at least once. About {{daily_published}} idea pins are published a day. Creators want, for their own pins, views per page and where viewers stop going forward, saves and outbound clicks per pin, and how each edit changed those numbers.
sections.problem: Design the data model for idea pins and their engagement. Cover: the pin, its versions (what was live when), pages with an identity that survives reordering, media assets and their processing states (a video page is shown only when its media is ready), tags at pin and page level, and how an edit creates a new version without losing what was live before. Then define the engagement events and facts: page views by page and by page position, forward progression from page to page, saves and outbound clicks per pin, all tied to the version that was live when they happened. Say how "the last page reached" is defined for a viewer session and how the creator's report shows a pin whose pages were reordered.
sections.constraints: Every engagement event can be tied to the exact version and page that was shown. Reordering pages must not move a page's history to a different page. Media that failed processing is never shown, and a pin is never published with a page whose media is not ready. A creator sees their own pin's per-page numbers; viewers appear only in aggregate. Edits never rewrite what an earlier version was.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, page counts and shares are hypothetical. A viewer moves forward and back through pages; a page view is logged each time a page is shown for at least a threshold you define. Product tags reference catalogue products by id; topic tags come from a fixed list. Each version is immutable once published.
sections.criteria: Pin, immutable versions and stable page ids kept apart, with positions on a version-page table; media assets with processing states and a publish rule that requires ready media; tags at the right level and versioned; engagement events that carry version, page and position; per-page and per-position metrics defined, including forward progression and the last page reached; late events for old versions attributed correctly; creator-only access to per-page numbers; retention and aggregation sized for the volume; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: If a page's media is replaced, is it the same page?
clarifications.a: Your call, stated. Many teams keep the page id and record a new media asset in a new version; then per-page history spans both media.

clarifications.q: Does a reorder create a new version?
clarifications.a: Yes. Any published change creates a new version; drafts are not versions.

clarifications.q: How are page views logged?
clarifications.a: Clients send a page-view event with the pin id, the page id, the page's position and the version id; events can arrive late and out of order.

clarifications.q: Can a creator delete a page?
clarifications.a: Yes. The page is absent from new versions; its history stays with earlier versions.

clarifications.q: What does "drop-off" mean?
clarifications.a: Define it. For example: among sessions that viewed page k, the share that never viewed a later position.

hints: Separate the pin (stable id), its versions (immutable snapshots with a published_at), and pages (stable ids) joined to versions through a version-page table that carries the position.
Engagement events carry the version id and page id that the client actually rendered; never infer them later from the "current" version.
Report per page id and per position separately: a reorder changes which page sits at position 3, not the history of either page.
followups: Show the rows for a pin with pages P1, P2, P3; the creator moves P3 to the front and replaces P2's video. What does version 2 look like, and what happens to P2's views?
A client that cached version 1 keeps sending events for an hour after version 2 is published. How does your model attribute them?
Define forward progression per page position for one version, and say what the creator sees when they compare version 1 with version 2.
A product tagged on page 4 is removed from the merchant's catalogue. What happens to the tag, to earlier versions, and to outbound clicks already counted?
At {{daily_published}} new pins a day with up to {{max_pages}} pages, which per-page event grain do you keep for how long, and what aggregate serves the creator report?

rules.ask: Storing pages as an array inside the pin row is simple. How does a page's view history survive when the creator reorders that array?
If position is the key for per-page metrics, what happens to page 2's history after page 4 is moved to the front?
An event arrives an hour late for a version that is no longer live. Which page did the viewer see, and how do you know?
A viewer swipes back from page 5 to page 2 and leaves. What is their last page reached, and what does your definition count?
A video page fails processing after the creator pressed publish. What does the version look like, and what do viewers see?

incidents: After a client release, page-view events carried the position but not the page id. For a week, pins whose pages had been reordered (about {{edited_share}} of idea pins are edited) showed one page's views under another page in creators' reports.

A video processing backlog let a version go live with a page whose media was still processing. Viewers saw a blank page, and forward progression past that page collapsed for pins with {{video_share}} video pages.
An edit job rewrote earlier versions in place to fix a typo in the tags, and the comparison between versions that creators rely on now shows identical versions.

templates.title: Shopping as data — merchants, catalogues, products and variants, product pins, and price and availability over time
templates.subtopic: catalogue feeds, variant groups, price and availability history, product pin identity

sections.scenario: Merchants upload product catalogues as feeds: one row per item with the merchant's item id, an item group id that ties variants (sizes, colours) together, title, link, image, price, an optional sale price with its start and end, currency, and availability (in stock, out of stock, preorder). Each merchant's feed is fetched again every {{feed_hours}} hours; a new upload can change prices, add or drop items, or re-use an item id for a different product. There are {{merchants}} merchants, {{catalogue_items}} items in total, and prices in {{currencies}} currencies. Each item becomes a product pin that pinners can save; pins show the price and availability, and saved product pins power features such as price-drop notices. Merchants want, in aggregate, impressions, saves and outbound clicks per product and per item group.
sections.problem: Design the data model: merchants and their catalogues, feed uploads and their processing outcome, products and variants (item groups), product pins and how a pin stays tied to the right product, and the history of price, sale price and availability. It must answer "what price and availability did this product pin show at a given time", "which items changed price in the last upload", "how long was this variant out of stock last month", and per-product engagement for the merchant. Say how a dropped item, a re-used item id and a bad upload (prices all zero, or half the catalogue missing) are handled.
sections.constraints: Money is stored as integers in minor units with the currency code; nothing is summed across currencies without an explicit conversion with a dated rate. Price shown on a date must be reconstructable. A bad upload must never wipe out a catalogue: an upload is applied only if it passes validation. A product pin never silently changes to a different product. Merchants see only their own catalogue's metrics; pinners appear only in aggregate.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, refresh cadence and currency counts are hypothetical. A sale price is valid only between its start and end times (this exercise's rule; check current docs for real feed specifications). Item ids are unique within a merchant, not across merchants. Feeds are full snapshots, not deltas.
sections.criteria: Upload rows kept immutable and separate from served product state and from attribute history; price, sale price and availability as validity intervals with the sale window honoured; integer minor units with currency, and dated conversion only in reports; item groups as attributes with history; a stable product key behind each pin and an explicit rule for dropped and re-used item ids; upload validation that blocks a bad feed and keeps the previous state; merchant-only access to metrics; a change-set estimate for the refresh cadence; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is the price shown the sale price or the regular price?
clarifications.a: The sale price while it is valid, otherwise the regular price, in this exercise. Store both.

clarifications.q: An item disappears from a feed. Is it deleted?
clarifications.a: Decide and state the rule. Common: mark it missing, hide its pin after a stated number of consecutive uploads without it, keep its history.

clarifications.q: Can an item move between item groups?
clarifications.a: Yes, merchants regroup variants. Pins and history stay with the item; the group is an attribute with history.

clarifications.q: How do we detect a re-used item id?
clarifications.a: You decide the signal, for example a different link and title with a matching id. Say what happens to the old pin.

clarifications.q: Do we keep every upload?
clarifications.a: You decide retention, but price history must be answerable for at least a year.

hints: Separate what the merchant sent (upload rows, immutable) from the product state you serve (current product rows) and from the history of the attributes that matter over time (price and availability intervals).
Most uploads change little. Store history as change intervals per item (valid_from, valid_to) produced by comparing an upload with the current state, not as a full copy per upload.
A product pin references a stable internal product key. Map (merchant, item id) to that key, and only re-point the mapping deliberately.
followups: Show the history rows for one variant whose price drops, goes out of stock, gets a sale price for a weekend, then comes back in stock at full price.
A merchant's upload arrives with half the items missing. What does validation check, what happens to the catalogue, and what does the merchant see?
A merchant re-uses item id 12345 for a different product. How do you detect it, and what happens to the saved pins and engagement of the old product?
With feeds every {{feed_hours}} hours across {{catalogue_items}} items, how big is the daily change set, and how do you compute it without a full comparison of everything?
A merchant asks for outbound clicks per item group across {{currencies}} currencies and a regrouping last month. Which grouping and which conversion do you use, and how is that labelled?

rules.ask: Which attributes trigger a new version: price, availability, title, image? What happens to your row count when a merchant changes a title in every upload?
A pinner asks why a product pin showed $40 yesterday and $55 today. With prices overwritten, how do you answer?
How do you store a price in a currency with no minor unit, and in one with three decimals? Where does rounding happen?
An item missing from one upload is back in the next. What happened to its pin and saves in the meantime?
Copying the full catalogue every {{feed_hours}} hours: what does that cost at {{catalogue_items}} items, and how do you answer "price on a date" from it?

incidents: A merchant's feed arrived with every price set to 0 after an export bug. The upload passed validation, product pins showed free items for one {{feed_hours}}-hour cycle, and price-drop notices fired for thousands of saved pins.
A merchant re-used item ids after a site migration. Saved product pins began to show different products, and a pinner who saved a lamp was notified about a price drop on a sofa.
An exchange-rate table was missing for one day, and a merchant report that summed outbound-click value across {{currencies}} currencies treated the missing rate as 1.

templates.title: Claimed websites and attribution — creators claiming domains, pins credited by claim, claims lost and re-verified
templates.subtopic: verification lifecycle, claim intervals, URL normalisation, crediting events by time

sections.scenario: A creator can claim a website they own by proving control of the domain, for example by adding a meta tag to the site or a record to its DNS (this exercise's model of verification; check current docs for the methods offered). Once a claim is verified, pins that link to that site are credited to the creator: the creator's analytics include impressions, saves and outbound clicks on every pin linking to the site, including pins other pinners created from the site's pages, and those pins can show the creator's name. {{claimed_domains}} domains are claimed and about {{linked_pins}} pins link to a claimed domain. Verification is re-checked every {{recheck_days}} days; if a check fails, the claim stays in force for a grace period of {{grace_hours}} hours (this exercise's rule) and is then lost unless a later check passes. A domain can be claimed by only one account at a time, a creator can release a claim, and a domain can later be claimed by someone else.
sections.problem: Design the data model for claims and for crediting. Cover: claim attempts and verification checks (method, result, time), the claim lifecycle (pending, verified, failing within grace, lost, released) kept as history, the intervals during which each account held each domain, how a pin's link is turned into the host that claims are matched against (case, a leading www., redirects, link shorteners, tracking parameters), whether subdomains are covered, and the fact tables that credit each engagement event to the creator whose claim was in force when it happened. Say what happens to creator analytics when a claim is lost, regained, or moves to another account.
sections.constraints: Credit is decided by the claim in force at the time of each event, not at the time the pin was created and not by today's claim. Claim intervals of one domain never overlap. A creator's past numbers never move to another account when the domain changes hands. A creator sees analytics only for pins credited to them; pinners appear only in aggregate. Verification evidence (the check results) is kept for audit.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, the re-check interval and the grace period are hypothetical. Engagement events arrive at least once and can be hours late. A link's host can be read from the pin's URL; following redirects needs a fetch, which is done by a separate crawler that you may assume exists and records the final URL with a time.
sections.criteria: Verification checks, claim state history and derived claim intervals kept apart; the grace period applied once with a precise end; intervals of one domain that never overlap; link-to-host normalisation as a versioned rule, with redirects and shorteners handled through recorded crawler results; a stated subdomain rule with the most specific claim winning; credit by an as-of join on event time, stored on the fact so history never moves; late events credited by their event time; creator-only access; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: During the grace period, is the claim in force?
clarifications.a: Yes. It ends when the grace period expires without a passing check, at that instant.

clarifications.q: Does a re-verified claim restore credit for the time it was lost?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. Events while no claim was in force are credited to nobody, and that is shown to the creator as a gap.

clarifications.q: Are subdomains covered?
clarifications.a: Decide and state the rule. A common choice: a claim covers subdomains unless a more specific claim on a subdomain is in force.

clarifications.q: Can two accounts claim the same domain?
clarifications.a: Not at the same time. A second account can claim it only after the first claim is released or lost.

clarifications.q: Do pins created before the claim count?
clarifications.a: Yes, from the moment the claim is in force. Credit is decided per event.

hints: Keep three things apart: verification checks (append-only evidence), the claim's state history, and the derived claim intervals (account, domain, valid_from, valid_to) that crediting reads.
Normalise each pin's link to a host once, store the result with the rule version that produced it, and re-derive when the rule changes.
Credit events with an as-of join of event time to claim intervals; store the credited account on the event fact so history never moves.
followups: A domain's check fails at 10:00 on day 3; the creator fixes the tag and a re-check they request passes at 09:00 on day 5. With a {{grace_hours}}-hour grace period, was the claim ever lost? The creator then releases it and another account claims it a week later. Show the intervals.
A creator's numbers show a dip. How does your model let them see that the dip is a lost claim and not fewer saves?
An event arrives eight hours late, after the domain changed hands. Who is credited, and how does your pipeline make sure the late event is not credited by today's claim?
The host normalisation rule changes to strip a new tracking redirect. Which pins change hosts, which facts are recomputed, and how is the restatement shown?
At {{linked_pins}} linked pins and billions of events a week, how do you do the as-of join cheaply, and where is the credited account stored?

rules.ask: The pin was created before the domain was claimed, and the domain later changed hands. Which creator does a save made last week credit under your design?
The domain moved to another account yesterday. What happens to the previous owner's numbers for last month if you join on the current claim?
Where is the grace period applied: in the claim state history, in the intervals, or at query time? What does an analyst see if they apply it again?
A host myexample.example and a claim on example.example. Does your suffix test credit it? Write the condition that does not.
The crawler re-fetches a short link and it now redirects to a different site. Which pin events move, and which stay?

incidents: A DNS provider outage made every check of a large hosting provider's sites fail for longer than the {{grace_hours}}-hour grace period. Thousands of claims were about to be lost at once; the team must decide whether to pause loss of claims or let them lapse.

A daily job credited events by joining pins to the current claim table. When a popular domain changed hands, the previous owner's dashboard lost months of history overnight and the new owner gained it.

A normalisation change stopped stripping www. for one week. Pins linking to www. hosts were credited to nobody, and about a fifth of credited outbound clicks disappeared for affected creators; checks run every {{recheck_days}} days did not notice because the claims were fine.

templates.title: Creator weekly metrics — impressions, saves and outbound clicks credited by the domain claim in force
templates.subtopic: as-of interval joins, half-open boundaries, host normalisation, most-specific match

sections.scenario: Creators can claim a website domain so that pins linking to it are credited to them in their analytics (this exercise's rule; check current docs). domain_claims holds one row per period during which an account held a domain: it starts at claimed_at and ends at released_at (NULL while it is still held). A domain can be released and claimed again later, by the same creator after a lapse or by another creator, sometimes at the very same instant. Each pin may link to a web page; {{host_rule}} pin_events holds impressions, closeups, saves and outbound clicks on pins. The data covers {{weeks}} weeks starting Monday {{first_monday}}; pins and claims can be older.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns creator_id, week_start, impressions, saves, outbound_clicks: one row per creator and week with at least one credited impression, save or outbound click, ordered by creator_id, week_start. An event is credited to the creator whose claim on the pin's host is in force at the event's occurred_at: claimed_at <= occurred_at and (released_at IS NULL or occurred_at < released_at). {{match_rule}} Events on pins without a link, or whose host is covered by no claim in force at that moment, are credited to nobody. week_start is the date of the Monday that starts the event's week in UTC. Closeup events are not counted, and a creator with only closeups in a week has no row for it.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Claims of one domain never overlap in time. Count events: each event_id is one event. The sample has {{claims}} claims, {{pins}} pins and {{events}} events; production has billions of events a week, so say how the query would scale.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, creators, domains and events; domains use the reserved .example suffix. Timestamps are UTC. A pin's link never changes after it is created.
sections.criteria: Credit by the event's time with a half-open claim interval (inclusive start, exclusive end); event types filtered before grouping; Monday UTC weeks; no rows for uncredited events or zero counts; host normalisation from the Hard level; at the hardest level, subdomains covered with a dot-anchored suffix test and one claim per event, the most specific; deterministic ordering; can explain how to make the as-of join scale and where the credited creator should be stored.

clarifications.q: A pin was created before its domain was claimed. Do its events count?
clarifications.a: Its events from claimed_at on do. Credit is decided per event, by the event's time, never by when the pin was created.

clarifications.q: The domain moved to another creator in the middle of a week. Who gets that week?
clarifications.a: Both, each for their own events. An event exactly at the moment of the change belongs to the claim that starts then, not the one that ends.

clarifications.q: Should I credit today's owner of the domain?
clarifications.a: No. Today's owner gets only the events from their own claim periods.

clarifications.q: Are saves counted per pinner?
clarifications.a: No. Count events; the table has one row per event.

clarifications.q: Does a week start on Sunday?
clarifications.a: No. Weeks start on Monday 00:00 UTC.

hints: Join events to pins, then to domain_claims on the host and on the time condition with the event's occurred_at. Filter the event types before grouping.
